Question:
Given three positive integers \(a,\) \(b,\) and \(c.\) Their greatest common divisor is \(D;\) their least common multiple is \(M.\) Then, which two of the following statements are true?

\((1)\) The product \(MD\) cannot be less than \(abc.\)

\((2)\) The product \(MD\) cannot be greater than \(abc.\)

\((3)\) \(MD\) equals \(abc\) if and only if \(a,\) \(b,\) \(c\) are each prime.

\((4)\) \(MD\) equals \(abc\) if and only if \(a,\) \(b,\) \(c\) are relatively prime in pairs. (This means: no two have a common factor greater than \(1.\))
Solution:
Prime factorization lets us compare the greatest common divisor, least common multiple, and product one prime at a time. Fix a prime \(p\), and arrange its exponents in \(a,b,c\) as
\[
0\le\alpha\le\beta\le\gamma,
\]
using exponent \(0\) when \(p\) is absent. The ordering may differ for different primes.

A common divisor can use only the smallest available exponent, so \(D\) has exponent \(\alpha\). A common multiple must contain the largest exponent, so \(M\) has exponent \(\gamma\). Thus the exponent of \(p\) in \(MD\) is \(\alpha+\gamma\), whereas its exponent in \(abc\) is \(\alpha+\beta+\gamma\).

Because \(\beta\ge0\), \(MD\) divides \(abc\), and both are positive integers. Therefore \(MD\le abc\), proving statement (2). Equality holds exactly when every middle exponent \(\beta\) is zero. This means that every prime divides at most one of \(a,b,c\), which is precisely the condition that the numbers are relatively prime in pairs. Hence statement (4) is also true. This reasoning includes inputs equal to \(1\), whose prime exponents are all zero.

To check the other statements, take \(a=b=c=2\). Then \(D=M=2\), so \(MD=4<8=abc\), disproving (1). The same example disproves (3), since all three inputs are prime but equality fails.

The two true statements are \(\boxed{(2)\text{ and }(4)}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
